description: The clarity of each yogic view is likened to a light of increasing strength and steadiness: a spark of straw fire, cow-dung fire, wood fire, a lamp, a gem, a star, the sun and the moon.
When the knot is broken in the sthirā view, all worldly activity appears to the wise like children playing at houses of dust.
Omniscience: knowledge of all substances in all their modes — past, present and future — at once, without senses or mind, with infinite perception, bliss and energy.
Direct supersensory knowledge: clairvoyance of material things within a range (innate in gods and hell-beings, acquired by others) and, in restrained ascetics, direct knowledge of others' thoughts.
Ascetics' attainments of a transformable body, a fiery body able to burn or bless, and a subtle projectable body sent to an omniscient to resolve a doubt.

At the end of life an omniscient whose remaining karmas are unequal expands his soul's space-points to fill the universe and contracts them again within a few instants, equalising the karmas before liberation.
notes: From the karma literature (Gommaṭasāra, Karmagranthas; not yet anchored to a U35 teaching).

description: At liberation the soul rises in one instant, straight up, like a flame or a gourd freed of its clay, and abides at the summit of the universe in its own knowledge and bliss.
Stages of mind known from practice: scattered and restless; coming-and-going with some bliss; clinging, steady and blissful; dissolved, very steady, with the highest bliss.
When the mind is left in indifference without being forced it becomes still of itself; in the no-mind state the yogin feels like one freed of a burden and experiences bliss beyond the senses.
notes: Hemacandra presents this as his own experience.

description: In the fire concentration the meditator sees flame rising from the syllable 'arhaṃ' and burning the eight-petalled lotus of the karmas and the body to ash.
Forcible restraint of the breath brings pain, and the pain disturbs the mind (Hemacandra's warning against making breath-control a path).
Signs in the breath, body, shadow and dreams are said to foretell the time of death, so that the practitioner may prepare with equanimity.
After reading the Samayasāra, Banārsīdās and his friends held only to the ultimate standpoint and abandoned discipline — a state he later describes as a fall into one-sidedness.
Taught the guṇasthānas by Rūpcand, Banārsīdās says his doubts ended and his mind became balanced, holding the pure self together with the stages of conduct.
The soul's longing for the Jina as its only beloved and husband, a love without beginning or end.
The tradition's account that Śrīmad Rājacandra remembered former lives from the age of seven (jātismaraṇa), later accompanied by self-realisation described in his letters.
notes: The tradition's account; not anchored to a U35 teaching (see trm:jatismarana, U34).

description: The state of the realised one 'whose condition, though in a body, is beyond the body' (Ātmasiddhi 142).
